Connected Media · Workflow platform on the canonical object model

Consolidated workflow requirements by phase and kind, and the platform analysis · Microsoft × Publicis Phase 0 · prepared for Bindu Chinnasamy · source: Core Application Requirements console (908 requirements), Phase 0 meetings, canonical model readout · November 2026

Summary

We read all 908 requirements in the Core Application Requirements console, the Phase 0 meeting record and the canonical-model work, and asked one question of each requirement: does it need a workflow, and if so which one and of what kind? This page consolidates the answer into a workflow catalogue by phase, groups it into eleven kinds, and works out what a workflow platform on top of the canonical object model must do and which platform fits best.

What the analysis shows

The workflow need is much wider than E8 shows
Publicis tagged 118 requirements to the workflow enabler (E8). Reading every requirement, 561 need a workflow: 252 are a workflow and 309 have a workflow step. Most of the extra need sits in data onboarding and overrides (step 10) and in the strategy steps.
Approval, lock and change are the spine
Approval & sign-off (90), lifecycle & lock (62) and change & re-approval (83) together are 235 of 561 workflow requirements (42%). They all act on versioned canonical objects, which is why the workflow layer must sit on the canonical model.
85 workflows, but only nine engine templates
The catalogue has 85 workflows across six phases and the cross-cutting platform. They fall into ten business kinds plus data pipelines, so nine reusable templates cover them; per-client differences are policy, not code.
Phase 1 and data carry the volume
223 workflow requirements belong to Foundation & Governance workflows. The largest single workflows are F10 Mapping review queue (50), F15 Metric override request & approval (45), S04 Strategy step confirm / lock / approve (42), F20 Access request, review & recertification (27), S06 Upstream change re-sync (stale source) (19).
The engine is the smaller part of the platform
Counting what each requirement needs, the audit store, the object lifecycle contract and the engine are each needed by about 260–280 requirements; tasks, events, notifications and policy by roughly 90–130 each. Every option needs these layers; only Camunda brings a task list and decision tables with it.
Owners and numbers are missing
Apart from one example in CP019 (an extra approver above $500K), no requirement names an approver matrix, a default threshold, an SLA value or a materiality level, and status words conflict across apps. These are configuration of the platform and need Publicis owners before any workflow can go live.

Recommendation

Build one workflow platform as eight layers on top of the canonical object model, on a code-first durable-execution engine running on AKS. The engine is the smaller decision: the lifecycle contract in each owning app, a versioned policy service for per-client chains and thresholds, one task inbox, notifications, the event link and an audit store are needed whichever engine is chosen, and they are where most of the work is.

Temporal (self-hosted)4.09
Durable Task (managed)4.03
Dapr Workflow3.90
Camunda 83.81
Logic Apps Std3.12
Power Automate2.63

Score out of 5: half from fit to the ten business workflow kinds (weighted by how many requirements each has), half from eight non-functional criteria taken from the meetings. Change the weights on the Platform options tab.

Temporal and Durable Task tie (within 0.1). Both are code-first, run their workers on Kubernetes and meet every workflow kind. The tie-breaker is who operates the engine before June:

  • Lean: Durable Task SDKs on AKS with the managed Durable Task Scheduler. Nothing extra to operate, Microsoft-supported, the same engine runs AI agents with human checkpoints, and the SDKs are open source. Keep the nine templates behind a thin internal interface so only they touch the engine; Dapr Workflow (same durabletask lineage, which Publicis asked about) is the portable exit.
  • Choose Temporal self-hosted on AKS if Publicis will run the cluster and values the most mature engine and full portability over a managed service.
  • Choose Camunda 8 only if process owners must draw new workflow shapes on a canvas; per-client chains, thresholds and SLAs do not need it, because the policy service makes them configuration.
  • Use Power Automate only for the M365 pilot. Publicis has said it does not want low-code workflow configuration, and a cloud-flow run cannot outlast 30 days.

How each phase, its canonical objects and the workflow engine fit together

Read it left to right. Something starts a workflow in a phase. The workflow runs on the one shared engine. When a decision is made, the engine asks the app that owns the canonical object to change its status. That app saves the change and publishes the milestone, and the event backbone carries it to the phases that listen.

One engine, every phase
The purple spine is the same engine. Each phase uses a few of the nine templates; differences between clients are policy, not code.
Objects stay with their owner
The engine holds the object ID and version, never the record. Only the owning app changes status (CP041, CP055), so the record and its event always agree.
Events connect the phases
A milestone saved in one phase (pink) starts, holds or reopens workflows in the phases that listen. Drafts, reminders and rejections never leave the phase.

Click a workflow to trace it: the arrows to its engine template and canonical objects, the objects themselves and the milestones it publishes stay lit while the rest fades. The bar above the diagram names them and links to the phase view and the workflow’s requirements; double-click a workflow to jump straight to its requirements. Dashed pink events are examples still to agree; solid ones are named in CP057. Owners follow the canonical model readout and still need Publicis agreement (CP055). Buy Authorized is proposed here: authorization is its own step (36) after Gate 2, and CP057 has no event for it.

  • Three workflows run outside the engine and plug into the same inbox and events: access on Entra ID Governance (F20), pipelines on the data orchestrator (F23, F24) and the mapping queue on Data Manager’s own queue service (F10).
  • Its milestones (Taxonomy Updated, Client Access Changed, Contract Approved, Source Live, Actuals Imported) feed every later phase.
Strategy & Planning · 8 workflows · 89 workflow requirements · 6 canonical objects moved
  • Brief, strategy outputs and the plan all follow the four-stage contract: confirm and lock = Final, client sign-off = Approved (CP051).
  • AI drafts in S01 and S04 run as agent steps inside the approval template; the AI can never approve (CP027).
  • Brief Approved starts strategy work and RFPs. Brief Revised goes through the change-impact service and S06 flags every step built on the old version.
Sourcing & Buy Authorization · 9 workflows · 46 workflow requirements · 7 canonical objects moved
  • Partner Sourcing owns RFPs, proposals, holds and awards. Gate 2 moves the Media Plan app’s Plan Version; Sourcing never edits the plan (PS051).
  • Holds are timer workflows: warn before expiry, then expire automatically. Hold Expired blocks Gate 2 until the plan is re-submitted (PS059).
Execution & Trafficking · 12 workflows · 61 workflow requirements · 8 canonical objects moved
  • Mostly integration sagas: the engine calls Prisma / OX, partner platforms and CM360 through connectors and waits for a receipt before anything counts as done (CP045, CP036).
  • Authorization (step 36) is the client step after Gate 2. Buy Authorized is a proposed event that starts bookings; CP057 does not name one.
In-flight Management · 9 workflows · 28 workflow requirements · 7 canonical objects moved
  • Alerts are raised by the data platform and monitoring; the engine only routes acknowledgement and escalation.

  • Work queues over actuals and invoices, plus a monthly timer for billing verification.
  • Close sign-off (R06) publishes Reconciliation Closed, which starts post-buy learnings (R07). An authorized role can reopen (AB013).
Cross-cutting platform · 16 workflows · 101 workflow requirements · 10 canonical objects moved
  • Platform governance on its own objects: schema versions, client configuration, releases, AI agents, incidents.
  • X06, X10, X12 and X13 are not workflows on a business object: they are the engine, notification, approval-chain and lifecycle services themselves.

Lines run only where a workflow changes an object’s status. Objects a workflow only reads are listed on its box as “also reads”. Dashed objects are owned in another phase but moved again here: Plan Version is the clearest case (Phase 2 build, Gate 2 in Phase 3, revision in Phase 5).

One approval, message by message: Gate 2 on plan version 03. The same pattern holds for every template; only the steps between “start” and “request transition” change.

The contract between an owning app and the engine

The engine offers the apps
StartWorkflowtemplate, object reference (type, ID, version), client, trace ID → run ID. The policy version is pinned at start.
Signaltell a waiting run something happened: an object changed, a receipt arrived, a client replied.
Cancelstop a run with a reason; open tasks close with it.
GetStatusqueued, running, waiting, completed, partial, failed, blocked, cancelled; current step, owner and next action (CP044).
Each owning app offers the engine
RequestTransitionobject reference, expected version, target state, decision reference, idempotency key → receipt, conflict or refusal.
GetObjectread-only view of the exact version, for task cards and checks.
Guardswho may move which state, mandatory fields, no self-approval, no silent skip or revert (CP051 #6).
Outboxstatus and the milestone event saved in one transaction, then published (CP057).

A workflow layer on top of the canonical object model

The canonical model says what a thing is, who owns it and which states it can be in. The workflow layer moves it between those states with people, timers, rules and other systems. The two meet in one place: the owning app. The engine asks; the app checks its guards, saves, and publishes the milestone.

The eight layers, and how many requirements lean on each

LayerWhat it doesGroundingRequirements needing it
Canonical objects & lifecycle contractEach object type has one owner app, a stable ID, a version and one lifecycle vocabulary. The owning app is the only writer of status.E2 · CP051 · CP054 · CP055 · CP056257
Workflow policy & configurationApprover chains, matrices, thresholds, materiality, SLAs, calendars, SoD rules per client. Versioned in the client configuration registry; each workflow pins the version it started with.CP019 · MP028 · PS060 · PA031 · CP10592
Durable workflow engineRuns workflow instances from a small set of templates: waits, timers, retries, sub-workflows, signals from events, AI steps. Holds references (IDs + versions), never business records.CP001 · CP044 · CP036 · CP045262
Human task service & inboxOne inbox across all apps: assign, claim, delegate, bulk act, due dates. Clients and vendors act through email + secure single-request links.CP016 · CP044 #6 · PS058 · CP086126
NotificationsIn-app, Teams and Outlook cards for staff; email for clients and vendors (no internal detail); digests and preferences.CP016 · DP081 · CP06296
Event backbone linkEvents start, hold, reopen or inform workflows. Owning apps publish milestones after they save (outbox). Change-impact service flags dependents.CP057 · CP042 · CP098117
Integration adaptersCalls to Prisma, partner platforms, ad servers, finance, ticketing and e-signature, with receipts and idempotency.CP045 · CP103 · PO00728
Audit, status & observabilityAppend-only decision log, workflow status API (queued … cancelled), SLA reporting, trace ID across phases, export for compliance.CP020 · CP044 #2 · CP021277

Counted from the capability tags on the requirements that need a workflow (one requirement can need several layers). The engine is one of eight; the lifecycle contract, audit and policy layers carry as much demand.

Design rules

1. Workflows act on canonical objects by ID and version
The engine stores references (object ID, version, policy version), never copies of business records. The owning app stays the system of record.
2. The owning app changes status; the engine asks
A workflow decision becomes a command to the owning app. The app checks guards, saves the new status and publishes the event from its outbox, so the record and the event never disagree.
3. Templates plus policy, not one-off flows
Nine engine templates cover every workflow in the catalogue. What differs per client (approvers, thresholds, SLAs) is configuration, versioned and pinned when a workflow starts.
4. Three status vocabularies, kept apart
Object lifecycle (Draft / In Progress / Final / Approved, CP051), workflow instance status (queued … cancelled, CP044) and task status (open / claimed / done). Most status conflicts in the requirements come from mixing these.
5. Milestones out, steps in
Only saved Final or Approved milestones become events. Submissions, reminders and rejections stay inside the workflow.
6. One inbox, many surfaces
Tasks live in one service; the apps, Teams and Outlook are just places to see and act on them. Clients and vendors get email and secure links, not licences.
7. People approve; AI drafts
AI is a named participant with its own identity. It can draft, recommend and submit, but never approve its own consequential action (CP027).
8. Use what already exists where it fits
Access requests and reviews on Entra ID Governance; data pipelines on the data orchestrator; Data Manager keeps its own review queue. They plug into the same inbox, notifications and events.

Keep three status vocabularies apart

VocabularyAnswersValuesRequirementsOwned by
Object lifecycleWhat state the business thing is inDraft → In Progress → Final → Approved (+ Locked / of record, Superseded, Retired)CP051, BW019, MP018, PS054Owning app
Workflow instanceWhere a run of a workflow isQueued, Running, Waiting, Completed, Partial, Failed, Blocked, CancelledCP044 #2Workflow engine
TaskWhere one person's to-do isOpen, Claimed, Delegated, Done (approved / rejected / returned), Expired, EscalatedCP001, CP019, PA031Task service
Request / data-onboarding statusRequest-specific stages shown to the requestere.g. DP079's 15 states: should map onto the three above, not be a fourth vocabularyDP079, DP081Owning app (view only)

One approval through the layers: Gate 2 on the tactical plan

  1. Planner confirms and locks plan version 03 in the Media Plan app; the plan moves to Submitted and locked. Object · MP018 · PS054
  2. The app starts an Approval workflow with plan ID, version 03 and the client; the engine pins policy version 7 for this client. Engine · Policy · CP044 · PS060
  3. Policy returns the chain: internal approver → finance (budget above the client threshold) → client. Policy · CP019 · PS060
  4. The task service opens a task for the internal approver; a Teams and Outlook card links to the exact version and evidence. Tasks · Notify · CP016 · DP081
  5. Approver opens the plan in the app and approves; no self-approval; the decision goes into the append-only log. Tasks · Audit · CP020 · CP027
  6. Finance approves. The client step sends an email with a secure single-request link; the client approves. Tasks · Notify · PS058
  7. The engine reports Approved to the Media Plan app. The app saves the status and writes Plan Approved to its outbox in one transaction. Object · Events · CP051 · CP057
  8. Plan Approved on the backbone starts the authorization and activation workflows in Execution & Trafficking. Events · Engine · PO001
  9. Mid-flight, a 20% cut crosses the materiality threshold: a revision workflow restarts approval for version 04; version 03 is kept. Engine · Policy · MP026 · MP028 · PS059

The Runtime contract tab shows the same approval as a message-by-message sequence.

Eleven kinds of workflow

Grouping the workflows by the shape of the work, not by the app, shows that a few patterns repeat everywhere. Each kind maps to one reusable engine template, so a new workflow is mostly configuration. “Primary” counts requirements whose main workflow need is this kind; “touched” also counts requirements where it is a secondary need.

KindPrimaryTouchedShare of workflow requirementsTemplateRuns on
K1 Approval & sign-off90159 16%Approval templateShared workflow engine + task inbox
K2 Lifecycle, lock & versioning62115 11%Lifecycle contract (library in each owning app)Owning app, using the shared lifecycle contract
K3 Hand-off, publish & kick-off3757 7%Event-started kick-off templateShared workflow engine, triggered by the event backbone
K4 Change control & re-approval83138 15%Change & re-approval templateShared engine + change-impact service
K5 Request & fulfilment5271 9%Request templateShared engine; Entra ID Governance for access
K6 Review queue & exception resolution5383 9%Work-queue template (queue service, not one workflow per item)Owning app queue + shared task inbox
K7 System transaction & integration2536 4%Saga / integration templateShared engine + connector adapters
K8 Recurring cycle, deadline & expiry3175 6%Timer / cycle templateShared engine
K9 Alert & incident3875 7%Alert routing templateMonitoring + notification service; engine only for escalation
K10 AI-assisted work with human checkpoints5262 9%Agent step inside any templateShared engine + AI platform
K11 Data pipeline run3858 7%Out of scope for the business engineData platform orchestrator (Dagster / Databricks jobs)
K1 · Approval & sign-off90 primary · 159 touched · 58 core
A person (or chain of people) decides on an exact version of an object.
Submit → pick chain from policy → task to approver 1 → … → approve / reject with reason → record decision → owning app changes status
The engine must provide
  • Approver chains and matrix per client (config, not code)
  • Branch by amount / budget size
  • No self-approval, independent approver
  • Delegate / reassign for PTO without breaking audit
  • Client or vendor as a step (email + secure link)
  • Waits of days or weeks, reminders, escalation
  • Decision tied to the exact object version and evidence
  • Append-only decision log
Most-tagged needs: Audit trail (38), Comments & decision log (31), Explicit status model (28), Decision pinned to exact version (26), Rules decide the path (21), Configurable approver chains / matrix (20)
Workflows with the most requirements of this kind:
F15 Metric override request & approval · 14S04 Strategy step confirm / lock / approve · 11F20 Access request, review & recertification · 10F25 Data service governance & criticality approval · 8B07 Tactical plan & Gate 2 approval · 7E09 Pre-launch QA go / no-go · 6S01 Brief intake, approval & lock · 5X05 AI capability / agent lifecycle approval · 5E06 Station creative clearance (TV) · 5F10 Mapping review queue · 5
K2 · Lifecycle, lock & versioning62 primary · 115 touched · 26 core
Governed status changes on a canonical object: Draft → In Progress → Final → Approved, confirm-and-lock, new versions.
Explicit, attributable transition → guard rules checked → version frozen when locked → milestone event published by the owning app
The engine must provide
  • One lifecycle vocabulary defined once per object type (CP051 #7)
  • Guards: who may move which state, mandatory fields, no silent skip or revert
  • Immutable locked versions; a change makes a new version
  • Owning app saves first, then publishes (outbox)
Most-tagged needs: Explicit status model (51), Audit trail (34), Confirm, lock, immutable version (25), Decision pinned to exact version (15), Flags dependents of a change (13), Rules decide the path (6)
Workflows with the most requirements of this kind:
S04 Strategy step confirm / lock / approve · 20S01 Brief intake, approval & lock · 5X05 AI capability / agent lifecycle approval · 5E06 Station creative clearance (TV) · 4F10 Mapping review queue · 4F26 Feed configuration lifecycle · 4B02 RFP / avails issue & partner responses · 4E07 Creative specs, assets & traffic instructions · 3X06 Cross-application orchestration (engine) · 3F08 Data dictionary & metric definition governance · 3
K3 · Hand-off, publish & kick-off37 primary · 57 touched · 25 core
An approved object is packaged for the next step or phase, published, and downstream tasks start.
Milestone event (e.g. Brief Approved) → package / snapshot by ID → start downstream workflow or tasks → receiver acknowledges
The engine must provide
  • Start a workflow from an event
  • Create tasks for the right teams from rules
  • Acknowledge receipt
  • Trace ID carried across phases
Most-tagged needs: Notify the person who must act (14), Audit trail (13), Confirm, lock, immutable version (13), Vendor / partner takes part (12), Explicit status model (12), Decision pinned to exact version (12)
Workflows with the most requirements of this kind:
S04 Strategy step confirm / lock / approve · 7B02 RFP / avails issue & partner responses · 6S06 Upstream change re-sync (stale source) · 6E07 Creative specs, assets & traffic instructions · 5S02 Brief kick-off & downstream tasks · 3E10 Verification, measurement & tag distribution · 3X10 Notifications & alerts (engine) · 2I01 Post-launch QA · 2E04 Buying platform entry & insertion orders · 2B06 Holds with expiry · 2
K4 · Change control & re-approval83 primary · 138 touched · 32 core
Revising something already approved or locked: size the change, re-approve if material, flag everything built on it.
Revision draft → materiality check (amount, %, client, channel) → re-approval if above threshold → new version → dependents flagged → accept / regenerate / diverge
The engine must provide
  • Materiality rules per client
  • Reopen or signal running workflows
  • Impact list of dependents (CP098)
  • Accept / diverge decisions logged
  • Pinned versions so in-flight work is not silently changed
Most-tagged needs: Flags dependents of a change (52), Audit trail (34), Explicit status model (20), Started or reopened by an event (20), Confirm, lock, immutable version (20), Decision pinned to exact version (19)

K5 · Request & fulfilment52 primary · 71 touched · 22 core
Someone asks for something (access, a new data source, a code or seat, an override) and it is triaged, approved, done and confirmed.
Request form → validate → route by type → approve → fulfil (people or systems) → confirm to requester → close, with SLA

Which platform fits best

The candidates are compared on two things: how well each serves the ten business workflow kinds (weighted by how many requirements each kind has), and the non-functional needs from the requirements and meetings. Data pipelines (K11) are left out: they run on the data orchestrator whichever engine is chosen. Scores are our assessment (1 = poor, 5 = strong); hover a cell for the reason.

Durable Task SDKs on AKS + Durable Task Scheduler

Code-first durable execution; open-source SDKs, Azure-managed state backend · Workers on AKS (or Container Apps) in the Azure spoke; managed scheduler in the same region
Strengths
  • Managed state store, dashboard and HA: nothing extra to operate before June
  • Open-source SDKs in .NET, Java, Python run on any compute, including Publicis' preferred Kubernetes
  • Same engine runs AI agents with human checkpoints (Microsoft Agent Framework durable extension)
  • Microsoft-supported service in a Microsoft-delivered programme; no per-user licence for clients or vendors
Watch-outs
  • The managed backend is Azure-only; a move off Azure means porting templates (for example to Dapr Workflow, same durabletask lineage)
  • Orchestration history kept up to 90 days (Dedicated), so the business audit trail lives in our own store
  • No authoring canvas: chains are configured in the policy service we build
Checked facts
  • SDKs are portable, open-source and run on Container Apps, Kubernetes or VMs; each connects to the Durable Task Scheduler as its managed backend · source
  • Dedicated SKU: up to 90 days retention, 2,000 actions/s per capacity unit, HA with 3 units · source
  • Durable extension for Microsoft Agent Framework: human-in-the-loop approvals and timed waits · source

Temporal, self-hosted on AKS

Code-first durable execution, open source · Temporal server + database on AKS in the Azure spoke (Temporal Cloud runs only on AWS / GCP)
Strengths
  • Most mature durable-execution engine: signals, updates, schedules, replay, workflow versioning
  • Open source (MIT) and Kubernetes-native: strongest portability and IP ownership
  • Team experience: John and Mak used it on Vodafone; Bindu’s team built an agentic workflow on it
Watch-outs
  • Publicis or Microsoft must run the cluster, its database and visibility store, with upgrades and HA
  • Temporal Cloud would take workflow data outside Azure
  • No authoring canvas (John Hauppa, 10 Nov): same policy service to build as Durable Task
Checked facts
  • Temporal Cloud service regions are AWS and GCP · source
  • OpenAI Agents SDK integration runs agents as Temporal Workflows · source

Dapr Workflow on AKS

Code-first durable execution in the Dapr sidecar (CNCF) · Dapr extension on AKS; workflow state in an Azure state store (for example Cosmos DB or PostgreSQL)
Strengths
  • Publicis asked whether to build on Dapr (Mark Agar, 27 Oct) to keep 250 future developers consistent
  • CNCF, runs on any Kubernetes; same building blocks for pub/sub, state and secrets
  • Engine built on durabletask-go: a portable exit for Durable Task code
Watch-outs
  • Younger workflow engine than Temporal or Durable Task; less tooling for operating long-running human workflows
  • We operate the sidecars and the state store
  • No authoring canvas
Checked facts
  • Engine runs in the Dapr sidecar, implemented with durabletask-go, built on Dapr actors; state lives in state stores · source
  • CNCF runtime with workflow SDKs for .NET, Java, Python, Go, JavaScript · source

Camunda 8, self-managed on AKS

BPMN / DMN process orchestration · Self-managed on AKS (Azure reference architecture); SaaS runs on GCP / AWS
Strengths
  • Business-readable BPMN models and DMN decision tables: the authoring canvas John asked for
  • Tasklist, Operate and Optimize included: inbox, operations, process analytics
  • Agentic orchestration connectors
Watch-outs
  • Production self-managed use needs the Enterprise licence
  • Heavier platform to run (cluster + secondary storage)
  • Mark Agar wants a build, not workflow configuration; Tasklist is weak for bulk review queues
Checked facts
  • Self-managed production use requires the Camunda Self-Managed Enterprise Edition · source
  • SaaS regions are on Google Cloud and AWS · source
  • Azure AKS reference deployment · source

Azure Logic Apps Standard

Low-code integration workflows, single-tenant · Workflow Service Plan / App Service Environment in the Azure region
Strengths
  • Hundreds of connectors (ServiceNow, DocuSign, SAP, Office 365): good as an integration adapter
  • Data stays in the region; VNet and private endpoints
  • Designer canvas
Watch-outs
  • Low-code is not what Publicis wants to lean on (Mark Agar, 5 Nov)
  • Per-client chains, materiality and versioned policy get hard to read and test in the designer
  • Not suited to high-volume human queues
Checked facts
  • Standard: single-tenant, data stays in the region; VNet and private endpoints · source

Power Automate + Dataverse

Low-code M365 / Power Platform flows · Power Platform environment (Publicis tenant)
Strengths
  • Fastest pilot; native Teams / Outlook approvals
  • Staff already have M365 licences for Teams and Outlook approvals
Watch-outs
  • Publicis: “not really looking for an implementation of SharePoint and a set of workflows” (Mark Agar, 5 Nov)
  • A cloud-flow run lasts at most 30 days including pending approvals; run history kept 30 days
  • Business data would sit in Dataverse, against each app owning its canonical objects; Power Platform licences for heavy use
Checked facts
  • Run duration 30 days including pending approvals; run retention 30 days · source

OptionWhy
AWS Step FunctionsMicrosoft builds on Azure services in this programme (Ronnie Yates, 3 Nov).
Dagster / Airflow for business workflowsPipeline orchestration; it does not address user-facing approvals (3 Nov recap). Keep for data pipelines (K11).
Durable Functions on Functions plansSame engine family, but Publicis prefers Kubernetes over serverless functions for long-term workloads (Ryan O'Hara, 3–4 Nov). Use the Durable Task SDKs on AKS instead.
Temporal Cloud / Camunda SaaSHosted on AWS or GCP, so workflow data would leave the Azure regions.

Do we need an engine, or just state in a database?

Simple approvals: state plus a task is enough
107 workflow requirements are approvals or status changes with no timers, escalation, retries or events. For these the team view that “approval is bookkeeping” holds: the owning app saves the decision and the task service tells people.
Durable execution is needed for the rest
244 workflow requirements need waits with reminders and escalation, timers and expiries, retries without duplicates, receipts from outside systems, schedules, SLAs, trace IDs or event-driven reopening. Building those on a database by hand is building an engine; CP044, CP045 and PA031 ask for them explicitly.

Who authors a workflow?

LevelWhoWhat they changeHow
PolicyPublicis administrators, per clientApproval stages and approver roles, conditions (amount, %, channel, plan status), optional client step, parallel or any-of approvers, SLAs, reminders, escalation, delegation, materiality thresholdsAdmin screens on the policy service; versioned in the client configuration registry with test, promote and roll back (CP019, PS060, MP028, PA031, CP105). Running workflows keep the version they started with.
TemplatesPlatform developersThe nine reusable shapes: approval, kick-off, change, request, work-queue escalation, integration saga, timer, alert escalation, agent stepCode, reviewed and versioned like any product code; new shapes are rare
Business logicApp teamsGuards and status transitions on their own canonical objectsThe lifecycle contract in each owning app (CP051)

This answers the concern that a developer should not write code every time a client needs a different approval flow (John Hauppa, 10 Nov), while keeping the product a build rather than low-code configuration (Mark Agar, 5 Nov). A drawing canvas is only needed if process owners must invent new workflow shapes themselves; that is the case for Camunda.

Access request & review workflowsReuse Entra ID Governance (access packages, reviews, PIM)SameE1 team
Data pipeline orchestrationKeep on the data orchestrator (Dagster / Databricks jobs); hand over by eventSameData platform team
Audit & SLA reportingBuild: append-only decision store + lakehouse copySameE9 team

When to choose differently

Portability across clouds becomes a hard requirement
Choose Temporal, self-hosted on AKS. Same code-first model and open-source licence; Publicis operates the cluster and its database.
Process owners must model and change workflows themselves
Choose Camunda 8 self-managed on AKS, with DMN tables for chains and thresholds. Budget for the Enterprise licence and a heavier platform.
The first release must stay inside M365
Use Power Automate + Dataverse for the pilot only. Plan the move before any approval can exceed 30 days or clients need to act.
Steps are integration-heavy (ticketing, e-signature, finance)
Add Logic Apps Standard as a connector adapter called by the engine; keep the workflow logic in the engine.
The work is a data pipeline
Keep it on the data orchestrator (Dagster or Databricks jobs). Hand over to business workflows by event: Source Live, Actuals Imported.
The work is an access request or review
Use Entra ID Governance (access packages, reviews, PIM) and show its tasks in the shared inbox.

Prove it: a three-week spike on four representative workflows

WorkflowKindsWhat it provesRequirements
Gate 2 tactical plan approval with client stepK1 + K4Chain from the policy service (internal → finance → client optional), threshold branch, client email + secure link, reject loop; then a revision crossing the materiality threshold restarts Gate 2. Build it on Durable Task and on Temporal to compare.PS054–PS060, MP018, MP028, CP019, CP020
Insertion order to Prisma with receipt, then amendment on Budget ChangedK7 + K3Idempotent send, receipt before done, retry, compensation; Budget Changed event reopens the order workflowPO007, PO017, CP036, CP045, CP057
Hold expiry and metric override requestK8 + K5 + K6Expiry timer with warnings and automatic release; override request to a reviewer queue with SLA and bulk actionsPS047, PS050, DP override set, PA031
AI-drafted optimisation with human approvalK10 + K1Agent drafts a budget shift with evidence; strategist approves; AI cannot approve; full traceRM045, RM047, CP027, CP044

Measure in the spike:

  • Time to build each workflow from the shared templates
  • An admin changes a client's approver chain with no deployment; running instances keep their pinned version
  • Version a template while instances are running
  • Export the decision log for one plan (audit)
  • Teams and Outlook cards, client email link
  • Failure drills: kill workers mid-run, replay, no duplicate orders
  • Operating effort: what it took to run Temporal on AKS vs the managed scheduler

Gaps, conflicts and questions

What reading every requirement surfaced: places where the requirements disagree, values nobody has stated, and workflows the process needs that no requirement defines. Each needs an owner before the platform can be configured.

Status words disagree across apps
CP051 defines Draft / In Progress / Final / Approved for every artifact. BW009 lists Draft, In Progress, Complete, Rejected for the brief, while BW010, BW019 and BW020 rely on Approved, Confirmed and Locked. DP079 defines 15 request states and DP075 adds Verification Failed, which DP079 does not list. Fix: keep three vocabularies (object, workflow, task) and map the rest onto them.
CP051BW009BW010BW019BW020DP079DP075CP044
No approver matrix, and many approvers unnamed
CP001 needs an approver matrix per artifact and client, and its story IDs (AM-4 … AM-35) do not match the epic numbering. Approvers are not named for MSA, SOW, staff plan, billing codes, go-live (CP081), the SoD matrix (PA022), restatements (RM018), metric stewards (RM004) or the “where required” strategy approvals (SP064, SP070, SP122).
CP001CP019CP081PA022RM018RM004SP064SP070SP122
Thresholds, SLAs and timers have no values
The only number is CP019’s example (> $500K adds an approver). Pacing alerts say “X%” (RM024); uplift approval (SP099), approval SLAs and escalation (SP147), station lead times (PO028), dormancy (PA020) and data cut-offs (DP047, DP053) are unset. MP028 makes materiality configurable but no defaults exist.
CP019RM024SP099SP147PO028PA020MP028
Re-approval rules conflict
PS059 sends the tactical plan back for re-submission after any hold, rate or proposal change, with no size test, while MP028 asks for materiality thresholds so small edits avoid re-approval. Agree which wins for Gate 2.
PS059MP028PS054
Trigger and publish order differ inside the brief
BW015’s story starts the kick-off on an approved brief, but its first acceptance criterion starts it for every created brief. BW016 publishes on approval while BW019 allows publishing only after confirm and lock. SP137 allows exporting an unconfirmed deck; SP151 blocks sharing until approval is recorded.
BW015BW016BW019SP137SP151
No event for client authorization, and no agreed object owners
CP057 names Plan Approved but nothing for the client authorization at step 36 (MP019, PS061), which is what lets bookings start (PO007 #1). The architecture proposes Buy Authorized as an example event. Object ownership in the new Architecture views follows the canonical model readout; CP055 still needs Publicis to confirm it, and CP054 leaves out RFP, proposal, hold, order line, creative and contracts.
CP057MP019PS061PO007CP055CP054
Step numbers out of date
PO007, PS056 and PS059 call Authorization step 34 (it is 36); PO010 calls Pre-launch QA step 45 (it is 47). Workflow definitions should reference step names, not numbers.
PO007PS056PS059PO010
Access requests in two queues
CP103 syncs access and service requests to the enterprise ticketing tool, while PA002–PA031 define approval, expiry and escalation in the platform. Decide which is the system of record.
CP103PA031PA002
Title and story mismatches on engine requirements
CP016 is titled “Design System” but defines notifications and may duplicate MB02; PA001’s story does not match its title; CP052 mixes Certified / Uncertified with Governed / Ungoverned.
CP016PA001CP052
Clients and vendors are rarely in the loop
Only a few dozen workflow requirements put a client or vendor in a step, mostly sourcing and trafficking (RFP responses, clearance) plus brief and Gate 2 sign-off. Commercial approvals with the client (CP019’s “Account Lead → Finance → Client”) are implied but not specified per artifact.
CP019BW020PS058CP086
